part_title: Prompt Caching, Distillation, LLM Evaluation and Prompt Versioning

scenes.title: Prompt caching and inference cost trade-offs
scenes.visual_overview: A Bedrock input-prefix cache can reuse eligible repeated context while each request still adds new tokens and generates a new answer.
visual_walkthrough: Left reused financial-assistant system prompt and long policy document
Bedrock prompt cache contains supported reusable prefix
Cache-hit arrow and new user-specific question enter foundation model
Output tokens remain newly generated
Worked illustrative first versus subsequent token counts; compare caching, RAG and model customization
scenes.visual_example: First request processes approximately 12,000 input tokens and 300 output tokens; later eligible cache hit reuses prefix with approximately 200 new input tokens plus 300 newly generated output tokens. These are illustrative uncached-token figures, not a reduction in context length.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Caching is useful with repeated eligible prefixes and supported models, subject to TTL, checkpoints, token thresholds and actual cache pricing; it is not RAG or fine-tuning.
scenes.narration: This slide explains why repeated large prompts can be expensive and when prompt caching helps. Start on the left. Many employees use the same financial-assistant instruction and a long shared policy document. Each user asks a different question, but the common prefix is identical. The arrow carries that content into Amazon Bedrock and the central prompt-cache panel. For supported models and configured checkpoints, the same eligible prefix can be reused instead of being processed from scratch every time. Follow the dotted cache-hit path toward the foundation model. The purple arrow underneath adds the new user-specific question, such as asking for the remote-work policy in three bullets. On the far right, the model still generates fresh output tokens for this request. In the worked example, the first request has about twelve thousand input tokens and three hundred output tokens. A later cache hit uses the same shared prefix and adds about two hundred uncached input tokens, while generating another three hundred output tokens. These figures are illustrative: the cached prefix still occupies context and real savings depend on model support, thresholds, cache duration and pricing. The lower comparison clarifies that retrieval, or RAG, fetches information at runtime, while model customization changes behavior through training. Prompt caching does neither. Choose it when requests frequently repeat a substantial identical prefix.

scenes.title: Model distillation versus other customization approaches
scenes.visual_overview: A five-stage pipeline transfers narrow-task behavior from a powerful teacher model into a smaller fine-tuned student, followed by careful evaluation.
visual_walkthrough: Teacher FM produces billing and shipping classification examples
Curated data panel checks accuracy, topic and balanced examples
Smaller student learns through fine-tuning
Held-out evaluation checks accuracy, precision/recall, safety and task success
Deploy narrow, potentially lower-cost model; compare RAG, prompt engineering, fine-tuning and pretraining
scenes.visual_example: A teacher labels 'I was charged twice' as Billing and 'When will my order arrive?' as Shipping. A student predicts Billing for a new support email with an illustrative 0.93 confidence.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Distillation can reduce narrow-task cost and latency, but student capability must be measured; supported teacher/student pairings and regions vary.
scenes.narration: This diagram illustrates model distillation: teaching a smaller model to perform a specific job using examples produced by a more capable teacher. Follow the five numbered panels across the top. First, the teacher foundation model classifies example support messages. The pictured email about being charged twice is labeled Billing; a delivery-date question is labeled Shipping. Second, we curate the generated input-output pairs, checking that the labels are accurate, relevant and reasonably balanced. Incorrect teacher answers would otherwise be taught to the student. Third, we fine-tune the smaller student model on that curated dataset, updating its weights for this narrow classification task. Fourth, the separate evaluation panel checks held-out cases the student did not train on. Accuracy, precision and recall, safety and real task success matter more than assuming the student is always equivalent to its teacher. Fifth, if those goals are met, the student can serve the targeted workload with potentially lower latency and cost. In the lower worked example, a new complaint about a double charge receives Billing as its predicted class, with an illustrative confidence score of zero point nine three. That score is not a guarantee. The comparison beneath distinguishes retrieval for current facts, prompt engineering for instructions, fine-tuning for learned behavior and pretraining for broader capabilities. Distillation is especially useful when a repeatable narrow task justifies building and validating a smaller model.

scenes.title: LLM-as-a-judge and application-level evaluation
scenes.visual_overview: An evaluator language model grades candidate answers against reference context and a rubric, while people and application metrics check usefulness.
visual_walkthrough: Test set includes password reset question, source article and additional support scenarios
Candidate model answers are produced by Model A or B
Evaluator LLM scores groundedness, relevance and safety from 1 to 5
Right result shows illustrative 5/5/5 and human spot check
Bottom application metrics include 92 percent task completion, 4.6 out of 5 satisfaction, and $0.008 per interaction
scenes.visual_example: A password reset response instructs users to open Sign in, select Forgot password and follow an emailed link; reference matches and the pictured rubric gives three illustrative 5s.
scenes.visual_synthesis: An LLM judge is a scalable signal, not a ground truth: calibrate with humans and examine bias, real task outcomes, response quality and cost.
scenes.narration: This picture shows how a second language model can help evaluate the answers produced by an AI application. Start at the left test set. The example asks how to reset a password, and its reference support article lists the expected steps: open the sign-in page, choose Forgot password, and follow the email link. Additional scenarios ask about canceled-order refunds and around-the-clock support. In the next purple panel, candidate systems such as Model A and Model B produce their answers. The displayed password-reset answer follows the reference instructions. Now move to the evaluator LLM. It grades each response using the three rubric dimensions shown below it. Groundedness asks whether claims are supported by the reference. Relevance checks whether the response actually answers the question. Safety checks for inappropriate or harmful content. The right panel displays example scores of five out of five on all three dimensions, plus a human spot check. These scores illustrate the method, not an official fixed Bedrock response schema or proof of flawless quality. At the bottom, application metrics show why evaluation must extend beyond wording: the picture reports illustrative ninety-two percent task completion, user satisfaction of four point six out of five, and cost per interaction of zero point zero zero eight dollars. A judging model can be biased toward particular phrasing, verbosity or model families, so calibrate its ratings against human reviewers and real task outcomes.

scenes.title: Prompt versioning with Bedrock Prompt Management
scenes.visual_overview: A repeatable six-stage prompt lifecycle uses templates, mutable drafts, testing, immutable published versions, deployment and monitoring.
visual_walkthrough: Template contains product, policy, tone and next_step variables
Mutable DRAFT and A/B/C variant testing
Save selected prompt as immutable version v2
Application invokes selected Bedrock prompt version
Monitor quality and optionally roll back to v1
Worked comparison v1 versus v2 and sidebar separates prompt changes from model training and knowledge-base updates
scenes.visual_example: A support template with product AWS Storage, return policy, friendly tone and next step is improved in v2 to request a concise answer and support-resource link; application can select v1 again if v2 underperforms.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Prompt Management versions instructions and variables, not model weights or knowledge-base documents; evaluate, deploy and roll back by referencing the desired version.
scenes.narration: This slide walks through the complete lifecycle of a reusable prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Begin at the left template. Instead of hard-coding one support question, the prompt uses placeholders for product, policy, tone and next step. The application supplies those values when invoking the template. Follow the numbered arrows. The DRAFT is editable. Developers test candidate variants A, B and C, compare the responses and choose the one that performs best. They then save that selected template as an immutable numbered version, illustrated by version two. The application references that version for live requests, and monitoring measures answer quality, feedback and business results. The arrow along the bottom loops back for further improvement. Now inspect the worked example: version one asks for a clear answer using the return policy and a friendly tone. Version two adds instructions to keep it concise and include a support-resource link when unresolved. Both use the same illustrated values, including the AWS Storage product and return policy. If version two performs worse, the application can roll back by referencing version one; the old immutable version does not need to be rewritten. The sidebar is the crucial distinction. Prompt versioning changes instruction templates, not model weights. Fine-tuning changes weights, and knowledge-base updates change retrieved documents. Choose versioning when you need reproducible prompt behavior, testing, controlled deployment and rollback.
